claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Fine-grained samples have a higher grain-boundary density than coarse-grained samples.
Increasing grain-boundary density lowers the nucleation barrier for secondary phases during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure.
Coarse-grained Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 preferentially retains its high-temperature BCC structure because it has fewer grain boundaries.
Prolonged high-temperature annealing produces the coarse-grained baseline.
Severe plastic deformation followed by post-deformation annealing can produce a fine-grained structure while relieving residual defects.
Slow cooling permits sufficient diffusion near critical transformation temperatures for the proposed phase transformation.
Grain-boundary interfacial energies promote secondary-phase nucleation during cooling.
Grain boundaries provide preferential nucleation sites at which the local free-energy barrier for phase transformation is reduced.
Higher grain-boundary density enhances diffusion and local transformation kinetics.
Under identical slow cooling and aging near 700 °C, fine-grained samples will develop a higher volume fraction of secondary phases than the coarse-grained baseline.
Under identical slow cooling and aging near 700 °C, fine-grained samples will develop a finer dispersion of secondary phases than the coarse-grained baseline.
The coarse-grained baseline is expected to retain largely the high-temperature BCC structure after slow cooling and aging near 700 °C.
The proposed grain-boundary effect applies when moderate cooling and thermal exposure enable diffusional transformations.
The proposed grain-boundary effect may not apply under extremely rapid quenching.
Significant extrinsic stress fields may independently drive phase transformations and obscure the proposed grain-boundary effect.
Residual stress and local compositional inhomogeneity may alter phase-nucleation and growth kinetics.
